## Asymmetric Action Abstractions

Uniform abstractions are restrictive in the sense that all units have their legal moves reduced to those specified by scripts. In this section we introduce an abstraction scheme we call asymmetric abstraction that is not as restrictive as uniform abstractions but still uses the guidance of the scripts for selecting a subset of promising actions.
The key idea behind asymmetric abstractions is to
reduce the number of legal moves of only a subset of the units controlled by player ii; the sets of legal moves of the other units remain unchanged. We call the subset of units that do not have their set of legal moves reduced the unrestricted units; the complement of the unrestricted units are referred as the restricted units.
###### Definition 2

An asymmetric abstraction Ω\\Omega is a function receiving as input a state ss,
a player ii,
a set of unrestricted units 𝒰i′⊆𝒰ir\\mathcal{U}^{\\prime}\_{i}\\subseteq\\mathcal{U}^{r}\_{i},
and a set of scripts 𝒫\\mathcal{P}.
Ω\\Omega returns a subset of actions of 𝒜i​(s)\\mathcal{A}\_{i}(s), denoted 𝒜i′′​(s)\\mathcal{A}^{\\prime\\prime}\_{i}(s), defined by the Cartesian product of the moves in ℳ⁡(s,u,𝒫)\\mathcal{M}(s,u,\\mathcal{P}) for all uu in 𝒰ir∖𝒰i′\\mathcal{U}^{r}\_{i}\\setminus\\mathcal{U}^{\\prime}\_{i} and of moves ℳ⁡(s,u′)\\mathcal{M}(s,u^{\\prime}) for all u′u^{\\prime} in 𝒰i′\\mathcal{U}^{\\prime}\_{i}.
Algorithms using an asymmetric abstraction Ω\\Omega search in a game tree for which player ii’s legal actions are limited to 𝒜i′′​(s)\\mathcal{A}^{\\prime\\prime}\_{i}(s) for all ss.
---
If granted enough computation time, optimal algorithms using Ω\\Omega derive stronger strategies than optimal algorithms using Φ\\Phi
(Theorem [1](https://arxiv.org/html/1711.08101#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1 ‣ Asymmetric Action Abstractions ‣ Asymmetric Action Abstractions for Multi-Unit Control in Adversarial Real-Time Games")).
In practice, due to the real-time constraints, algorithms are unable to compute optimal strategies for most of the decision points. We analyze empirically, by comparing GABP to GAB and SABP to SAB, which abstraction scheme allows one to derive stronger strategies.
### Strategies for Selecting Unrestricted Units

In this section we describe three strategies for selecting the unrestricted units. A selection strategy
receives a state ss and a set size NN and returns a subset of size NN of player ii’s units. The selection of unrestricted units is dynamic as the strategies can choose different unrestricted units at different states.
Ties are broken randomly in our strategies.
1. 1.
More attack value (AV+). Let
a​v​(u)=d​p​f​(u)h​p​(u)av(u)=\\frac{dpf(u)}{hp(u)}. AV+ selects the NN units with the largest a​vav-values, which allows search algorithms to
provide finer control to units with low h​php-value
and/or large d​p​fdpf-value.
This strategy is expected to perform well as it might be able to preserve longer in the match the units which are about the be eliminated from the match and have good attack power.
2. 2.
Less attack value (AV-). AV- selects the NN units with the smallest a​vav-values. We expect this strategy to be outperformed by AV+,
as explained above.
3. 3.
Random (R). R randomly selects NN units at si​n​i​ts\_{init} to be the unrestricted units. R replaces an unrestricted unit that has its h​php-value reduced to zero by randomly selecting a restricted unit. This is a domain-independent strategy that in principle could be applied to other multi-unit domains.
## Empirical Methodology

We use SparCraft111

github.com/davechurchill/ualbertabot/tree/master/SparCraft as our testbed, which is a simulation environment of Blizzard’s StarCraft.
In SparCraft the unit properties such as hit points are exactly the same as StarCraft. However, SparCraft does not implement fog of war, collisions, and unit acceleration \[ [2013](https://arxiv.org/html/1711.08101#bib.bibx4 "")\]. We use SparCraft because it offers an efficient forward model of the game, which is required by search-based methods. All experiments are run on 2.66 GHz CPUs.
### Combat Configurations

We experiment with units with different h​php, dd, and rr-values. We use ↑\\uparrow to denote large and ↓\\downarrow to denote small values. Also, we call uu a melee unit if uu’s attack range equals zero (r=0r=0), and we call uu a ranged unit if uu is able to attack from far (r>0r>0).
Namely, we use the following unit kinds: Zealots (Zl, ↑\\uparrowh​php, ↑\\uparrowdd, melee), Dragoons (Dg, ↑\\uparrowh​php, ↑\\uparrowdd, ranged), Zerglings (Lg, ↓\\downarrowh​php, ↓\\downarrowdd, melee), Marines (Mr, ↓\\downarrowh​php, ↓\\downarrowdd, ranged).
We consider the combat scenarios where each player controls units of the following kinds: (i) Zl; (ii) Dg; (iii) Zl and Dg; (iv) Zl, Dg, and Lg; and (v) Zl, Dg, Lg, and Mr.
We experiment with matches with as few as 6 units
and as many as 56 units on each side.
The largest number of units controlled by a player in a typical StarCraft combat is around 50 \[ [2013](https://arxiv.org/html/1711.08101#bib.bibx4 "")\]. The first two columns of Table [2](https://arxiv.org/html/1711.08101#Sx6.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Asymmetric versus Uniform Abstractions ‣ Empirical Methodology ‣ Asymmetric Action Abstractions for Multi-Unit Control in Adversarial Real-Time Games") show the 20 combat configurations used in the experiments. The number of units is distributed equally amongst all kinds of units.
---
NOKAV and Kiter are scripts commonly used for inducing uniform abstractions \[ [2013](https://arxiv.org/html/1711.08101#bib.bibx4 "")\]. NOKAV assigns a move to uu so that uu does not cause more damage than that required to set an enemy’s unit h​php to zero. Kiter allows uu to attack and then move away from its target.

### Searching in Uniformly Abstracted Spaces

Churchill and Buro (?) introduced PGS, a method for searching in uniformly abstracted spaces. Algorithm [1](https://arxiv.org/html/1711.08101#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Uniform Action Abstractions ‣ Asymmetric Action Abstractions for Multi-Unit Control in Adversarial Real-Time Games") presents PGS, which receives as input a state ss,
player ii’s and −i-i’s set of ready units for ss (𝒰ir\\mathcal{U}^{r}\_{i} and 𝒰−ir\\mathcal{U}^{r}\_{-i}),
a set of scripts 𝒫\\mathcal{P}, a time limit tt, and an evaluation function Ψ\\Psi. PGS returns an action aa for player ii to be executed in ss.
PGS selects the script σ¯i\\bar{\\sigma}\_{i} (resp. σ¯−i\\bar{\\sigma}\_{-i}) from 𝒫\\mathcal{P} (lines [1](https://arxiv.org/html/1711.08101#alg1.l1 "In Algorithm 1 ‣ Uniform Action Abstractions ‣ Asymmetric Action Abstractions for Multi-Unit Control in Adversarial Real-Time Games") and [2](https://arxiv.org/html/1711.08101#alg1.l2 "In Algorithm 1 ‣ Uniform Action Abstractions ‣ Asymmetric Action Abstractions for Multi-Unit Control in Adversarial Real-Time Games")) that yields the largest Ψ\\Psi-value assuming player ii executes an action composed of moves
computed with σ¯i\\bar{\\sigma}\_{i} for all units in 𝒰ir\\mathcal{U}\_{i}^{r} (resp. 𝒰−ir\\mathcal{U}\_{-i}^{r}), assuming −i-i (resp. ii) executes an action selected by the NOKAV script.
Action vectors aia\_{i} and a−ia\_{-i} are initialized with the moves computed from σ¯i\\bar{\\sigma}\_{i} and σ¯−i\\bar{\\sigma}\_{-i}.
Once aia\_{i} and a−ia\_{-i} have been initialized, PGS
iterates through all units ukiu\_{k}^{i} in 𝒰ir\\mathcal{U}\_{i}^{r} and tries to greedily
improve the move assigned to ukiu\_{k}^{i} in aia\_{i}, denoted by ai​\[k\]a\_{i}\[k\].
Since PGS only assigns moves to units given by scripts in 𝒫\\mathcal{P}, it considers only actions in the space induced by a uniform abstraction. PGS evaluates aia\_{i}
for each possible move σ¯​(s,uki)\\bar{\\sigma}(s,u^{i}\_{k}) for unit ukiu^{i}\_{k}.
PGS keeps in aia\_{i} the action found during search with the largest Ψ\\Psi-value.
